newsitem.title: UK: Cricket-English game seeks fresh profile.
newsitem.headline: Cricket-English game seeks fresh profile.

text.p: The traditional pre-season rituals of an English cricket summer are here. Daffodil-yellow Wisdens poke out from the bookshelves, bets are struck and grown men practise imaginary off-drives in their office corridors.

That this is currently one of the sunniest Aprils in recent memory and the Australians are due on May 13 only adds to the sense of a fine summer ahead. It all goes to show what tricks a spell of good weather and blossom in the hedgerows can play on a nation's memory.
Barely three months ago, to the rest of the world's amusement, English cricket was at such a low ebb it could have sought sponsorship from one of Britain's increasingly unreliable water companies.

The winter tour to Zimbabwe should have been a perfect chance to refresh the test team's desultory overseas record; instead it provided a well-documented PR debacle of such proportions a trip over Victoria Falls in a barrel might have been as comfortable.

Improvement in New Zealand was scarcely enough to ensure a hero's welcome on their return home, but when the curtain rises on the six-test Ashes series in June the cast is likely to be virtually unchanged.

Mike Atherton was reappointed captain for the summer on Monday and coach David Lloyd will be alongside him. Both of them could do with a victory in the first test at Edgbaston starting on June 5; they also know there are some patriots who feel England's long-term hopes may be best served by another crushing defeat.

For among the cosy rituals of spring, there is a realisation this is a watershed season for the first-class game and beyond. New English Cricket Board supremo Lord MacLaurin has already warned that "amber lights are flashing over our game" and Wisden editor Matthew Engel argues that English cricket, unless it embraces radical change, is in a "potentially catastrophic" state.

At least there will be an overdue experiment with floodlights in some one-day matches; certainly no previous season has begun with the test squad embarking on a two-day 'charm' course to improve their image.

A company specialising in motivational courses for businessmen and headed by former England rugby captain Will Carling has been called in and the team could be in for a shock. Part of the programme is said to include a dinner where the players will be expected to stay sober and make polite conversation.

Atherton has even promised to stay clean-shaven for the remainder of his time as England captain, but the wider reaction to Engel's critical comments in Wisden has been instructive. Instead of agreeing with him, the establishment has largely closed ranks and hidden behind the healthy gate receipts expected from the Ashes series.

How many of the paying spectators will be children, let alone those from poorer families with increasingly little exposure to cricket in schools, remains a moot point and there is still complacency in many pavilions.

Moves, for example, to amalgamate local leagues in Lancashire and thus provide a more streamlined route to the top for younger players have been rejected and engaging overseas players is still the main priority at many counties.

Fitness levels, at least, appear to be changing with Somerset, under new coach Dermot Reeve, paying out bonuses to those players who meet their individual targets regardless of what they do with bat or ball.

Maybe English cricket has changed over the last 20 years. Or maybe not. "Miraculously we have some cricket....as we were batting first I escaped from the freezing, draughty wooden pavilion and slipped into Oxford just before the start. A spot of shopping, a hasty Wimpy with totty-spotting out of the window, then rush back to the ground in case we were 25 for eight....mercifully, rain returned after lunch to draw the curtain over three forgettable days."

Such were the joys of April cricket in 1977 as experienced by former England captain Bob Willis in his Warwickshire days. Compare his account with promising young Hampshire opener Jason Laney, offering his opinions on the game in the 1997 Cricketers' Who's Who.
"Too much cricket and tea is not long enough," writes Laney, picked to play for the Rest against England A later this week. "Fielding is very trying at times -- need more rain."
English cricket in safe hands? Or merely a case of lulling Australians into a false sense of security? The next five months will provide the answer.
